rationale: On 453 held-out CONFLICTS items jev-1.13.0 is confidently wrong (mean confidence on errors 0.56-0.58, up to 0.99-1.00; probability gap -0.48 to -0.50) and the correct/wrong confidence gap is only 0.073-0.166, so the author judges confidence too weak for confidence-gated automation without external calibration (Sec. 3 findings a-c, Sec. 6; read via the author's GitHub report mirror because the alphaXiv PDF was not retrievable).

JevLite 3-seed ensemble reaches AUROC .974 on 577 held-out turn decisions, non-inferior to the MiniMax-M3 LLM judge at the preregistered .02 margin (diff +.027 [-.011,.065]) with 100% vs 82.3% legit-call accuracy, though not significantly better than a ModernBERT encoder (Sec. 5, Table 2).

Jev coded 195,857 Texas crash narratives at $0.154 per thousand (projected $774 for 5.0M) with AUROC 0.908 vs human labels, but its probabilities fail calibration (Spiegelhalter -5.3, slope 1.63) and become usable only after recalibration on 2,416 human judgments; one frontier LLM gains 0.059 AUROC and the other is indistinguishable (Abstract, Sec. 4.1-4.4, Sec. 6).

For thresholding/selecting statements for inspection, Jev's raw sentence ECE is 0.119 (NLI judge 0.105) and the authors state task-specific isotonic calibration (ECE 0.124 to 0.008) is needed before using probability thresholds; RadMatch (LLM-based) is better on clinically significant errors (Sec. 5.6, Sec. 6).

Single-run case study on a 13-vulnerability target: the harness with Jev hit 9/13 scenarios vs 10/13 without and recalibrated 9 of 22 severities, but the BOLA case required domain-specific evidence engineering and the author states results are observations without statistical power (Sec. IX, Tables VI-VIII, Table X).

LAVOIR decisions match the Bayes ceiling on seen schemas (gap -0.006, ECE .013-.015) and asking tracks value only after adding a Gini cap and per-group temperatures, while zero-shot schemas stay 15 pts below ceiling and on ABCD the model is wrong in 19% of cases at confidence >=0.99 (Table 1, Sec. 7.1-7.2, Limitations).

On jev-1.13.0 one unverified observer opinion appended to the state flips 12.1% of 812 decisions (+11.1 pp over the noise floor), tied with the strongest injected command (10.1%), while rewording stays within 1.2 pp of re-run noise (Abstract, Sec. 4.2, Sec. 6).

Under attack a 0.8 confidence gate lets 12.6% of flips through (24.1% for observer opinion), attack-time confidence (AUROC 0.885) adds little over clean confidence (0.808), Noul has no confidence and a review band misses ~52% of its flips, and opinions push 38.0% of confident answers into review (Sec. 4.4).

Jev's negation-complementarity violation is 0.064 vs 0.293 (first-token) and 0.122 (verbalized) for Qwen3.8-27B, yet Jev is not coherent: violations are ~5x repeat noise and its three single-label probabilities sum to 1.14 (Abstract, Sec. 5, Conclusion).

SubJudge (9B, one forward pass) matches or beats frontier LLMs on PLURIHARMS (individual MAE 0.1659 vs 0.168 Kimi-K3) and iNews arousal/dominance (MAE 0.7530/0.6960 vs 0.8929/0.6995) with 1.29-261x lower latency than Qwen3.5-9B, supporting high-traffic personalized deployment (Sec. 3.1, 3.3, Table 6).

Under changed/runtime-declared questions the fine-tuned Laya returned its training answer for 98-99.5% of changed questions (insensitivity, not robustness) while Jev and AnyJev acted wrongly on at most 0.143/0.137, so Laya's rewording stability (<=0.4 pt) is not semantic robustness (Abstract, Sec. VI-C Table V, VI-F).

The preregistered frozen confidence gate on Laya beats random escalation decisively but misses its accepted-set error target out of sample on both tracks, so a deployment must re-validate the threshold on fresh data (Abstract, Sec. 7 E5).

Decomposing decisions through broad categories yields substantial incoherence for both systems (category TV 0.219-0.349 Jev, 0.424-0.689 Laya) and reconstruction cuts Jev's CLINC150 accuracy by 22.9 pts while raising Laya's by 21.3 (with Laya's MASSIVE ECE rising 0.046 to 0.124) over 72,000 questions (Abstract, Sec. 9).

On MetaMedQA Jev 1.13 is better calibrated than GPT-6 Sol (ECE 0.063 vs 0.146) but this gives no selective-prediction advantage, DiagnosisArena discrimination is poor (AUROC 0.645 vs 0.768), and it chose 'I don't know' for only 10.5% of 162 unanswerable questions (GPT-6 Sol 8.6%) (Abstract, Results).

On 1,916 CyberSecEval items in 50-way CWE classification Jev beats all six open-weight LLMs on every metric but trails GPT-5.6-Sol on Top-1 and Macro-F1 while leading on Top-3/Top-5 with near-identical MRR (Abstract, Sec. IV-A Table I).

In the preregistered Jev supplement on public-policy texts all five European source-position interactions are below 0.05 (largest -0.0314) and the US interaction is -0.0197 vs -0.154 to -0.449 for chat models, but the author states this does not establish debiasing given a different rubric and scores concentrated mid-scale (Sec. 4.4 Table 2, Fig. 2, Appendix).

Across ten corpora in six languages Jev reaches the lowest aggregate VA RMSE (1.0645) and beats fine-tuned Llama-3.3-70B/GPT-OSS-120B on extraction (52.09/44.06 cF1), but only with corpus-specific supervised calibration (halving raw error) and language-group models, with the weakest result on Chinese laptop (39.43 vs 53.08) (Abstract, Sec. 3, Sec. 4.3-4.4).

PACT's raw holdout ECE is 10.8% and becomes 7.9% only after a fitted contextual temperature (whose shape is unstable across runs), and 28% of errors (16/58) are made with confidence >=0.9 (Sec. VI-C, Table III, Sec. VI-E).

On Chinese CJ-Bench general tasks off-the-shelf typed models are weak (Laya Multilingual 40.22%, SemIF 44.21%) vs Jev 68.35%, and Chinese-Jev reaches 69.20%/ECE 3.78% only after Chinese-specific pre-training, with legal/finance specialists still below Jev; typed models beat Qwen3.5-2B (32.95%) (Tables 1-2, Sec. 4.2).

With 3 seeds and paired tests, RLCD's single-query confidence ranks errors far better than GRPO+TS, RFT+TS and SFT+TS (GSM8K-Verify AURC 0.034 vs 0.061; 81% vs 19% of items decidable at 5% error; MMLU-Pro 28% vs 0-16% at 20% error) at equal or higher accuracy (Sec. 5.1, Table 1).

A rerun of 5 RLCDAlignBench legs reproduces AUROC within a 0.0036 median difference (0.53-0.97), but thresholds do not transfer: F1 at 0.5 rises by a median +0.254 only after fitting thresholds on 10 labels, and TensorTrust-hijack (AUROC 0.948) has 8.8% recall at t=0.5 (README results 1-2, threshold table).

Laya-style RLCD training leaves raw outputs over-sharp (shipped raw ECE 0.466, 0.081 only after temperature scaling; fitted T rises 1.2 to 1.7 with noise), and the report concludes calibration comes from distillation plus temperature scaling, with CE-only at least as good on every proper score (README; docs/paper/main.tex Abstract, Intro, Conclusion).

The reproducible 30-record CSJN pilot (frozen questions, hashed manifest, order-stable 93.3%) is auditable, but Jev area accuracy is 60% (Kev 20%) vs 96.7% for rules, with errors at confidence 0.99-1.00 (12/16 correct at >=0.90), so the note marks legal conclusions ESCALATE (Resultados, Estado).

Methods note only: no live Jev call was evaluated and the 14/14 passing synthetic tests concern the export/question-proposal software contract, so there is no typed-model result to code (Abstract, Sec. 5, Sec. 7 item 1); non-empirical for detector coding.

On 7 benchmarks (n=500-600 each) Jev has the highest AUROC of every cheap-tier LLM on all binary tasks, is never significantly worse than a cheap-tier model, and beats or ties GPT-5.4 on all tasks, losing only to Claude Sonnet 4.6 on ANLI-R3 and HaluEval-Dialogue (Tables 2-3, Sec. 3.1).

As a prompt-injection detector Jev reaches AUROC 0.994 vs 0.892-0.969 for cheap-tier/GPT-5.4 judges (tie with Sonnet 0.997) and stays within a 0.010 spread across four wordings, though no adaptive attack on Jev itself was run and batching 8 short items costs -0.018 AUROC (Tables 2-3, 13, Sec. 3.3).

The local typed judge (Laya) collapses when it must notice absence or mismatch (no_support 0.309, explicit_contra 0.273 vs explicit_support 0.991, n=220 each) and scores 0.567 vs the LLM's 1.000 on 1,100 binary verifications and 0.225 vs 0.75-0.90 on 77-class intent (Sec. 6.0-6.2).

Self-reported fields cannot be trusted for audit: the access-layer 'probability' is P(selected option) and flips every false-answered item, truncation flags are wrong in both directions, and 'conflicted/undecided' labels are unreachable; the same P(true) trap recurs on the LLM side (Sec. 3.2-3.5, 3.4.1).

On 270 constructed authorization cases x3 repetitions Jev has lower permission Brier than GPT-4.1 mini (0.0263 vs 0.0555) and no false allows, but ties DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, permits fewer authorized actions (295/345 vs 315/345), and denies 18/357 approvable holds vs 1-2 for the LLMs (Abstract).

Bajev is a deterministic rule-based Kleene three-valued agent engine (105 tests, 100-record formal corpus, zero false certainty) that contains no Jev or other typed decision model, so there is no typed-model result to code (Sommario/Abstract, Sec. 2, Sec. 15).

For Kev-0.8B under 15 attacks per item, a coverage-based threshold sent every attacked wrong answer to review, but a fixed 0.8 threshold at raw temperature let three confident errors pass, the protection was a side effect of confidence dropping for any added text, and attacks forced unnecessary reviews (Abstract).

Across 26,796 calls in three scripts Jev's sovereignty status index is 0.40/0.26/0.40 (below every generative model) and it picks PRC formulations in Simplified-Chinese forced choice and under a Beijing asker, yet it never chose a Taiwan-under-China label in practical labeling (Claude Sonnet 5: 42% in Simplified Chinese) and was fastest/cheapest (paper.en.md Abstract, Sec. 4.2-4.7).
